History and Physical (H&P – Detailed)

Consult Summary:
65-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes awoke one hour ago with painless inability to move his left arm, left-sided facial tingling, mild dysphagia, and dysarthria; emergency ambulance arranged for suspected acute stroke.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Sudden loss of movement in left arm on waking this morning (≈1 h before call).  
• Course: Persistent; no improvement; speech difficulty worsening during call.  
• Associated symptoms:  
  – Tingling on left side of face since onset.  
  – Mild dysarthria (speech slower, requires more effort).  
  – Mild swallowing difficulty (spilled drink).  
• Denied/Not present: Left-leg symptoms, facial droop noticed by patient, limb pain, discoloration, coolness, headache, loss of consciousness.  
• Precipitating/relieving factors: None identified; slept in usual position.  

Past Medical History:
• Type 2 diabetes mellitus.  
• Hypertension.  

Medications:
• Metformin – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Losartan – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Amlodipine – dose/route/frequency not documented.  

Allergies:
• Penicillin (reaction details not stated).

Social History:
• Lives alone.  
• Former smoker (quantity/quit date not documented).  
• Alcohol: “A few pints of beer” on weekends plus “a couple” during the week.  
• No other substance use mentioned.

Family History:
• Father with unspecified heart disease.  
• No other familial illnesses reported.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded (telephone consultation).  
• General / Neurologic: No in-person exam possible; patient reports persistent left arm paralysis, facial tingling, dysarthria; no self-observed facial asymmetry.

Investigations:
• None prior to call.  
• Emergency ambulance dispatched for hospital evaluation and imaging per stroke pathway (imaging not yet performed).

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
Acute focal neurological deficit most consistent with an acute cerebrovascular event (likely ischemic stroke) requiring emergent in-hospital assessment and potential reperfusion therapy.

DDx Integration (aligned with transcript):
1. Acute ischemic stroke – sudden focal deficits, vascular risk factors, ongoing symptoms.  
2. Intracerebral hemorrhage – hypertensive risk and abrupt deficit; no headache or altered consciousness reported.  
3. Transient ischemic attack – similar presentation but deficits persisting and worsening.

Issue 1: Suspected acute stroke
• Assessment: Sudden painless left arm paralysis with facial sensory change, dysarthria, dysphagia in high-risk patient.  
• Plan:  
  – Ambulance arranged immediately; patient instructed to unlock door and wait seated in hallway.  
  – Telephone clinician to remain on line until EMS arrival.  
  – Anticipate hospital stroke team review, urgent brain imaging (CT/CTA) to differentiate ischemic vs hemorrhagic event and determine eligibility for thrombolysis/thrombectomy.  
  – Patient kept NPO; advise against driving or independent travel.  
  – Document exact time last known well (on waking ≈1 h prior).  
  – Communicate allergy (penicillin) and medication list to receiving team.

Issue 2: Chronic conditions (hypertension, type 2 diabetes)
• Assessment: Long-standing vascular risk factors; control status not discussed today.  
• Plan: Defer routine management; to be revisited after acute episode, including review of BP, HbA1c, medication adherence, and lifestyle counseling.

Issue 3: Medication & allergy reconciliation
• Assessment: Incomplete dosing information.  
• Plan: Confirm full medication list, dosages, and allergy specifics during inpatient evaluation.

General plan items:
• Ensure next-of-kin notification if needed (patient lives alone).  
• Safety net: Advise patient to seek immediate help if symptoms change while waiting; EMS already en route.  
• Follow-up: Outpatient review after hospital discharge to manage stroke risk factors and rehabilitation needs.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: No vital signs or objective neurological exam (telephone limitation); medication doses/frequencies not documented.  
● No transcript/DDx conflicts noted.  
● Transcript quality: Clear; purely audio-based, limiting physical findings.
